## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.38677.025](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.38677.025)

In the interests of transparency, eLife includes the editorial decision letter and accompanying author responses. A lightly edited version of the letter sent to the authors after peer review is shown, indicating the most substantive concerns; minor comments are not usually included.

Thank you for submitting your article "Current and future goals are represented in opposite patterns in object-selective cortex" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by three peer reviewers, including Floris P de Lange as the Reviewing Editor and Reviewer #1, and the evaluation has been overseen by Sabine Kastner as the Senior Editor. The following individual involved in review of your submission has agreed to reveal their identity: Brad Postle (Reviewer #2).

The reviewers have discussed the reviews with one another and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this decision to help you prepare a revised submission.

Summary:

van Loon et al. examine working memory representations of information that is either currently relevant (current) or will be relevant later (prospective). Using fMRI, they find that both types of working memory can be decoded from activity patterns in mid-level visual activity patterns. Strikingly, activity patterns were opposite for these two types of memory, with information that will be needed to accomplish a future goal, but not the most proximal one, represented in a format that is anticorrelated with format in which it will be represented when it is of highest relevance.

All three reviewers were enthusiastic about the aims of the study. There was however considerable debate about whether the results could indeed be interpreted as 'coding prospectively relevant information', or whether they could be equally well represent BOLD undershoot (reviewer 1) or attentional suppression (adaptation) of the unattended working memory (WM) item and/or class (reviewer 3).

Essential revisions:

It will be essential to satisfactorily rule out the alternative interpretations of the data put forward by reviewer 1 (point 1 and 2) and reviewer 3.

Reviewer #1:

van Loon et al. examine working memory representations of information that is either currently relevant (current) or will be relevant later (prospective). Using fMRI, they find that both types of working memory can be decoded from activity patterns in mid-level visual activity patterns. Strikingly, activity patterns were opposite for these two types of memory.

This is an interesting study, on the currently 'hot topic' of where and how visual information is maintained in working memory in the human brain. The paper is well written and coherent, and the analyses are expertly done and clear. I am however worried about some alternative explanations for the results that may ultimately render them rather hard to interpret.

1) Can the results be explained by BOLD undershoot?

During the prospective trials, the participants see an exemplar of the category of interest (e.g., a cow) and the flower, and then they see a cue that tells them to first focus on the flower. The null hypothesis (i.e., no sensory activity pattern for items that only become relevant later) would dictate that activity in the 'cow area' would simply decline, and become active again only during search display 2. Under this null hypothesis, cow voxels would have negative values during search display 1, which would explain why cross-classification results in below-chance performance.

The authors swiftly dismiss this possibility, because, as Figure 2—figure supplement 1 shows, overall BOLD signal in the prospective condition actually goes up. However, what is plotted here is mean BOLD signal of the entire pFS area. Naturally, the flower search display will generate a large BOLD signal (in e.g. flower voxels). I think it is quite plausible that the results are explained by a BOLD undershoot of the relevant voxels, which is masked by a BOLD activation by a concomitant activation of other visually response voxels.

2) Can the results be explained by systematic differences in search display 1 between current and prospective trials?

Another alternative explanation (of which I'm less sure it holds water, but I thought it may be good to mention it anyway) of the anti-decoding during search 1, is that prospective trials are trials in which the search 1 display is always the 'flower search display'. Current trials are trials in which something else than flowers is presented. Is it possible that the below chance decoding means that flowers don't resemble the other categories? In other words, is it possible that below chance decoding has nothing to do with the memorized target, but with the presented search display? (which is systematically different between conditions?)

3) Design choice

The authors designed their task such that one target was 'of interest' (could be of three categories) whereas the other was always exactly the same item (the flower). I am wondering whether this is a good design choice. One of the potential problems of this design choice is already mentioned in point 2. But it seems to create other forms of imbalance. For example, a 'prospective trial' may be more difficult than a 'current' trial. In prospective trials, there is a longer WM load, in current trials there is a reduced WM load (because the flower doesn't really require holding in WM, as behavioral results also show).

I don't really understand what advantage the current design has, over a design in which e.g. two exemplars would be shown from the three categories employed by the authors. This would be a more balanced design, and it would allow the authors to truly compare current vs. prospectively relevant items, in a design in which these trials are of equal difficulty.

Reviewer #2:

"Current and future goals are represented in opposite patterns in object-selective cortex," van Loon, Fahrenfort, Olivers. This manuscript introduces what may well come to be accepted as an important principle in the representational dynamics of information held in versus out of the focus of attention in visual working memory, with information that will be needed to accomplish a future goal, but not the most proximal one, represented in a format that is anticorrelated with format in which it will be represented when it is of highest relevance. The approach taken by the authors represents an important advance, in that it addresses how information is maintained in different states of priority, rather than "just" where. (Questions of 'where' can be interesting, but only if they give insight into/constrain models of mechanism, and this field has matured to the point where questions of 'where in the brain' no longer offer much of an advance.) Overall, the manuscript is very clearly written and argued, and my comments will mostly highlight points where clarity could be improved.

Figure 2A: It appears that, by TR4 following the cue, the prospective category is at baseline – if so, this could be consistent with a stimulus encoding response that then returns to baseline (as opposed to the prospective category being "actively" (my term, but the authors' implication) sustained across the initial delay).

Figure 3B: This is a nice visualization. It could provide more information if the individual exemplars were identified (as, e.g., 1, 2, 3, 4 rather than four undifferentiated green dots). What's not clear to me, however, is whether any quantitative and/or inferential information is conveyed by the lines that cross in the middle of each MDS plot for Search 1 and Search 2.

"Next we wanted to investigate what turns a currently relevant into a prospectively relevant representation." This misrepresents what was accomplished in the analyses that follow, which were more along the lines of 'tracking what transformation a representation undergoes when transitioning from currently to prospectively relevant." Indeed, it is noted in the Discussion that "A crucial question that our data does not answer is what the exact mechanism is behind this transformation."

For the analyses illustrated in Figure 4, more information is needed. First, what condition labels are used for the three sets of t-values in each plot? E.g., for "cow," are the betas from the cow regressor from the GLM used for all three plots (Current Same, Prospective Same, Prospective different)? If this is true, it's not surprising that there's very limited variance across voxels in the latter two conditions. Would the regression be more interesting if it was "fair" to the Different category by using its regressors? Also, how does this analysis reconcile with the idea of an opposite representation? E.g., why isn't the slope of Prospective Same of the same value as Current Same, but opposite in sign? A separate question is how interpretable the classifier weights are. With logistic regression, the importance of any given voxel can vary markedly depending on the level of sparsity that is imposed (i.e., depending on the lambda term in the regression model). Haynes's group has described a way to get unequivocal importance values from SVM, but I'm not familiar with a comparable metric for logistic regression. If such a diagnostic can be extracted from logistic regression it would be of considerable interest, and so should be detailed.

"We found that object category information was stronger for pFs, visual cortex and IPS than for RMF, whereas the impact of relevance (Current vs. Prospective) was apparent in all ROIs throughout the trial." This is an important point, and addresses a question of considerable current theoretical interest (and controversy), and so more information should be included – enough to support critical evaluation of this statement.

Reviewer #3:

van Loon and colleagues present the results of an elegant fMRI study designed to test for representational differences/similarities in coding scheme for items in working memory with different priority status (immediately relevant vs. prospectively relevant). The study is well-conceived, well conducted and well-motivated to tackle an important problem. The analyses are clear and appropriate, however the results are somewhat surprising. The authors report a literal reversal in pattern during search in the irrelevant display. Even more surprising, this occurred in both the first and second search position (i.e., even after the non-relevant item could be forgotten). The authors present these results very clearly, and provide at least two interpretations: top-down control (attention suppression?) or neural adaptation, favouring the latter.

A major question left unresolved is whether this adaptation (or top-down suppression) is item specific or general to the whole class of stimuli (category specific). Obviously this is a trickier analysis, but theoretically tractable and worth reporting whether or not it is possible. The results would be very informative, especially interpreting the effects within a working memory framework.

In general, the authors do a good job handling what feels like unexpected results; however, I think there is room to be a bit more upfront with the initial hypotheses. They are relatively clear that they did not expect a pattern reversal, and especially not during the second search. For clarity, I think it would be worth explicitly stating the initial hypotheses regarding the first delay period (presumably there is a case for qualitative different formats in preparation for search).

claims.claim: Prospective memory representations which could initially no longer be decoded during a working memory delay period could successfully be reconstructed after applying a brief burst of transcranial magnetic stimulation.

claims.claim: Enhanced decoding of a memorized oriented grating occurs shortly after observers are presented with a visual pattern that is neutral with respect to the memorized orientation.

claims.claim: The standard synaptic potentiation mechanism predicts that the altered pattern of responsivity directly follows the pattern of activity during encoding of the item, thus predicting a high degree of similarity between the active and the silent representation when revived.

claims.claim: Differently prioritized items in memory can be stored through similar patterns of firing activity, with the only difference being the degree of activation.
claims.source: Instead, they argued for a single maintenance mechanism in which differently prioritized items in memory are stored through similar patterns of firing activity, with the only difference being the degree of activation.
claims.evidence: This refers to an alternative theoretical model proposed by Schneegans and Bays (2017).

claims.claim: The revival of a memory can be explained by selectively boosting the still present, but lowered activity, rather than by the reconstruction from hidden states of responsivity.
claims.source: Their model simulations provide a proof of concept that the revival of a memory can be explained by selectively boosting the still present, but lowered activity, rather than by the reconstruction from hidden states of responsivity.
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical claim based on model simulations by Schneegans and Bays (2017).

claims.claim: Currently relevant items are represented more strongly in posterior brain areas (notably visual cortex).

(2018), who found currently relevant items to be represented more strongly in posterior brain areas (notably visual cortex), while prospectively relevant items were represented more strongly in frontal regions (notably the Frontal Eye Fields).

claims.claim: Prospectively relevant items are represented more strongly in frontal regions (notably the Frontal Eye Fields).

(2018), who found currently relevant items to be represented more strongly in posterior brain areas (notably visual cortex), while prospectively relevant items were represented more strongly in frontal regions (notably the Frontal Eye Fields).
claims.evidence: This finding is attributed to Christophel et al. (2018).

claims.claim: Studies have not directly compared the representational pattern of current and prospective memories.
claims.source: Although crucial for current theories of working memory, so far, studies have not directly compared the representational pattern of current and prospective memories.
claims.evidence: This identifies a gap in the literature that the current study addresses.

claims.claim: During the Delay prior to search, within-relevance decoding resulted in significant above chance object category decoding when the variable template was currently relevant in Experiment 1.

claims.claim: During the Delay prior to search, within-relevance decoding resulted in significant above chance object category decoding when the variable template was prospectively relevant in Experiment 1.
claims.source: As can be seen in Figure 2A and B, during the Delay prior to search the within-relevance decoding resulted in significant above chance object category decoding both when the variable template was currently relevant (t(1,23) = 8.18, p < 0.001, d = 1.67) and when prospectively relevant (t(1,23) = 5.67, p < 0.001, d = 1.16).
claims.evidence: This is an fMRI decoding result from Experiment 1 with statistical support and reference to Figure 2.

claims.claim: Decoding performance was higher when the item was currently relevant than when it was prospectively relevant during the Delay in Experiment 1.
claims.source: Notably, decoding performance was higher when the item was currently relevant than when it was prospectively relevant (Current vs. Prospective: t(1,23) = 3.22, p = 0.004, d = 0.66), consistent with its importance for the upcoming search task.

claims.claim: Object-selective cortex is sensitive to object category as well as task-relevance prior to search.
claims.source: Thus, object-selective cortex proves sensitive to object category as well as task-relevance prior to search.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the decoding results during the delay period.

claims.claim: During the delay prior to search, the representational pattern of the category was similar regardless of the current or prospective status of the object in Experiment 1.
claims.source: These results indicate that during the delay prior to search, the representational pattern of the category was similar regardless of the current or prospective status of the object.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion from the cross-relevance decoding analysis in Experiment 1.

claims.claim: In the Search 1 interval, clear decoding of the object category was observed when currently relevant in Experiment 1.
claims.source: As can be seen in Figure 2A and B, in the Search 1 interval we observed clear decoding of the object category when currently relevant (vs. 33.33%: t(1,23) = 11.57, p < 0.001, d = 2.36), and this was stronger than when the object was prospectively relevant (between-condition comparison: t(1,23) = 9.42, p < 0.001, d = 1.92).
claims.evidence: This is an fMRI decoding result from Experiment 1 with statistical support and reference to Figure 2.

claims.claim: Decoding of currently relevant objects during Search 1 was stronger than when the object was prospectively relevant in Experiment 1.

claims.evidence: This is an fMRI decoding result from Experiment 1 with statistical support and reference to Figure 2.

claims.claim: The prospective category could be decoded during the first search in Experiment 1.
claims.source: Importantly, we were still able to also decode the prospective category during the first search (vs. 33.33%; t(1,23) = 1.90, p = 0.035, d = 0.39).
claims.evidence: This is an fMRI decoding result from Experiment 1 with statistical support.

claims.claim: The prospective category re-emerges when observers are actively searching for an unrelated target.
claims.source: In other words, the prospective category re-emerges when observers are actively searching for an unrelated target.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the decoding results during Search 1.

claims.claim: Below-chance decoding performance was observed during Search 1 in the cross-relevance decoding scheme in Experiment 1.
claims.source: Remarkably, here we observed below-chance decoding performance during Search 1 (CP: t(1,23) = −4.79, p < 0.001, d = −0.98, and PC: t(1,23) = −3.67, p = 0.001, d = −0.75).
claims.evidence: This is an fMRI decoding result from Experiment 1 with statistical support.

claims.claim: Current and prospective representations of the same object category were represented through opposite multivariate patterns during Search 1 in Experiment 1.
claims.source: In addition, the fact that decoding was below chance suggests that current and prospective representations of the same object category were represented through opposite multivariate patterns.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the below-chance decoding results.

claims.claim: Currently relevant representations remained constant from delay to search in Experiment 1.
claims.source: Thus, while currently relevant representations remained constant from delay to search, the prospective representation was transformed from being similarly represented prior to search to being differently represented during search for the currently relevant item, followed by a reactivation for the second task.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion from the cross-temporal generalization analysis in Experiment 1.

claims.claim: The prospective representation was transformed from being similarly represented prior to search to being differently represented during search for the currently relevant item, followed by a reactivation for the second task in Experiment 1.
claims.source: Thus, while currently relevant representations remained constant from delay to search, the prospective representation was transformed from being similarly represented prior to search to being differently represented during search for the currently relevant item, followed by a reactivation for the second task.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion from the cross-temporal generalization analysis in Experiment 1.

claims.claim: Strong decoding of the category of the prospective target was observed during Search 2 when it had become currently task-relevant in Experiment 1.
claims.source: As expected, here we saw the pattern reverse (see Figure 2A and B). In the within-relevance decoding scheme, we observed strong decoding of the category of the prospective target, which by now had become currently task-relevant (against chance, 33%: t(1,23) = 9.86, p < 0.001, d = 2.01).
claims.evidence: This is an fMRI decoding result from Experiment 1 with statistical support and reference to Figure 2.

claims.claim: Above-chance decoding was observed for the first target during Search 2 even though it was no longer relevant in Experiment 1.
claims.source: Nevertheless, and unexpectedly, we also observed above-chance decoding for this first target during Search 2 (t(1,23) = 3.30, p = 0.002, d = 0.67, blue).
claims.evidence: This is an unexpected fMRI decoding result from Experiment 1 with statistical support.

claims.claim: Below-chance decoding was found during Search 2 in the cross-relevance decoding scheme in Experiment 1.
claims.source: Moreover, the cross-relevance decoding scheme also shows a pattern similar to what was observed during Search 1 (Figure 2C and D; and see also Figure 2—figure supplement 2A generalization across time). We found below-chance decoding in the same time range for both classification schemes (CP: t(1,23) = −4.65, p < 0.001, d = −0.95 and PC: t(1,23) = −4.49, p < 0.001, d = −0.92).
claims.evidence: This is an fMRI decoding result from Experiment 1 with statistical support and reference to figures.

claims.claim: Throughout the course of the trial, the neural representations moved from predominantly category space during the Delay period prior to search to predominantly relevance space during the two searches in Experiment 1.
claims.source: As can be seen from Figure 3A and B, throughout the course of the trial the neural representations moved from predominantly category space during the Delay period prior to search to predominantly relevance space during the two searches.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion from the representational dissimilarity analysis with reference to Figure 3.

claims.claim: Prior to search, objects grouped largely according to category, irrespective of relevance in Experiment 1.
claims.source: Prior to search, objects grouped largely according to category, irrespective of relevance.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the representational dissimilarity analysis in Experiment 1.

claims.claim: During Search 1, a clear relevance-driven distinction emerged between the neural object category representations in Experiment 1.
claims.source: During Search 1, a clear relevance-driven distinction emerged between the neural object category representations.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the representational dissimilarity analysis in Experiment 1.

claims.claim: Currently and prospectively relevant objects from the same category were represented as the most dissimilar during Search 1 in Experiment 1.
claims.source: More interesting though is the finding that currently and prospectively relevant objects from the same category were represented as the most dissimilar, as is illustrated by the representations taking opposite corners in the MDS plot in Figure 3B.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the representational dissimilarity analysis with reference to Figure 3B.

claims.claim: During the Delay prior to the first search, same category representations were more similar than different category representations across relevance in Experiment 1.
claims.source: During the Delay prior to the first search, as expected, same category representations were more similar than different category representations across relevance (t(1,23) = −5.82, p < 0.001, d = −1.28, as performed on Fisher-transformed 1-rho values).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from the representational dissimilarity analysis in Experiment 1.

claims.claim: During Search 1, prospective targets differed most from current targets when they belonged to the same category, more so than when they belonged to different categories in Experiment 1.
claims.source: In contrast, during Search 1, prospective targets differed most from current targets when they belonged to the same category, more so than when they belonged to different categories (t(1,23) = 3.06, p = 0.005, d = 0.64).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from the representational dissimilarity analysis in Experiment 1.

claims.claim: During Search 2, no longer relevant targets were less similar from relevant targets when they belonged to the same category, than when they belonged to different categories in Experiment 1.
claims.source: Likewise, during Search 2, no longer relevant targets were less similar from relevant targets when they belonged to the same category, than when they belonged to different categories (t(1,23) = 4.75, p < 0.001, d = 0.97).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from the representational dissimilarity analysis in Experiment 1.

claims.claim: Participants were equally accurate at finding the template object regardless of the search order in Experiment 2.
claims.source: The fact that participants were equally accurate at finding the template object regardless of the search order and that they were slower in the template search when performed second (i.e., Prospective condition) suggests that the quality of the memory representation did not decay when it had to be postponed, but reactivating it for Search 2 required additional time.
claims.evidence: This is a behavioral finding from Experiment 2.

claims.claim: Participants were slower in the template search when performed second (i.e., Prospective condition) in Experiment 2.
claims.source: The fact that participants were equally accurate at finding the template object regardless of the search order and that they were slower in the template search when performed second (i.e., Prospective condition) suggests that the quality of the memory representation did not decay when it had to be postponed, but reactivating it for Search 2 required additional time.
claims.evidence: This is a behavioral finding from Experiment 2.

claims.claim: The quality of the memory representation did not decay when it had to be postponed in Experiment 2.
claims.source: The fact that participants were equally accurate at finding the template object regardless of the search order and that they were slower in the template search when performed second (i.e., Prospective condition) suggests that the quality of the memory representation did not decay when it had to be postponed, but reactivating it for Search 2 required additional time.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the behavioral results in Experiment 2.

claims.claim: Reactivating the prospective memory for Search 2 required additional time in Experiment 2.
claims.source: The fact that participants were equally accurate at finding the template object regardless of the search order and that they were slower in the template search when performed second (i.e., Prospective condition) suggests that the quality of the memory representation did not decay when it had to be postponed, but reactivating it for Search 2 required additional time.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the behavioral results in Experiment 2.

claims.claim: There was significant above-chance object category decoding for all relevance conditions (Current, Prospective, and Irrelevant) during the Delay in Experiment 2.
claims.source: There was significant above-chance object category decoding for all relevance conditions: Current (t(1,24) = 10.76, p < 0.001, d = 2.15) Prospective (t(1,24) = 5.88, p < 0.001, d = 1.17) and Irrelevant (t(1,24) = 5.61, p < 0.001, d = 1.12).
claims.evidence: This is an fMRI decoding result from Experiment 2 with statistical support.

claims.claim: The difference between Current and Irrelevant decoding during the Delay was significant in Experiment 2.
claims.source: Pairwise comparisons revealed the difference between Current and Irrelevant to be significant (t(1,24) = 3.74, p = 0.001, d = 0.74).
claims.evidence: This is an fMRI decoding result from Experiment 2 with statistical support.

claims.claim: The difference in decoding accuracy between the Current and Prospective conditions during the Delay was not significant in Experiment 2.
claims.source: In contrast to Experiment 1 though, the difference in decoding accuracy between the Current and Prospective conditions was not significant (t(1,24) = 1.33, p = 0.193, d = 0.26), nor was there a significant difference between the Prospective and Irrelevant conditions (t(1,24) = 1.39, p = 0.175, d = 0.27).
claims.evidence: This is an fMRI decoding result from Experiment 2 with statistical support.

claims.claim: During the delay prior to search, the representational pattern of the memorized object category was similar regardless of the current, prospective or irrelevant status of the object in Experiment 2.
claims.source: Taken together, these results indicate that during the delay prior to search, the representational pattern of the memorized object category was similar regardless of the current, prospective or irrelevant status of the object.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion from the cross-relevance decoding analysis in Experiment 2.

claims.claim: Decoding accuracy for the current template was above chance during Search 1 in Experiment 2.
claims.source: Decoding accuracy for the current template was above chance (t (1,24) = 9.47, p < 0.001, d = 1.89) and significantly higher than for both the prospective template (t(1,24) = 5.53, p < 0.001, d = 1.10) and the irrelevant item (t(1,24) = 7.29, p < 0.001, d = 1.45).
claims.evidence: This is an fMRI decoding result from Experiment 2 with statistical support.

claims.claim: The prospective category could be decoded at above-chance levels during Search 1 in Experiment 2.
claims.source: More importantly, and in line with Experiment 1, we were able to decode the prospective category at above-chance levels during Search 1 (t(1,24) = 3.35, p = 0.003, d = 0.67).
claims.evidence: This is an fMRI decoding result from Experiment 2 with statistical support.

claims.claim: Decoding of the Irrelevant category remained at chance during Search 1 in Experiment 2.
claims.source: At the same time, decoding of the Irrelevant category remained at chance (t(1,24) = 0.60, p = 0.550, d = 0.12), and was significantly weaker than for Prospective condition (t (1,24) = 2.27, p = 0.032, d = 0.45).
claims.evidence: This is an fMRI decoding result from Experiment 2 with statistical support.

claims.claim: Information about the prospective template can be recovered while participants perform a different search task, whereas completely irrelevant categories are no longer decodable.
claims.source: Thus, information about the prospective template can be recovered while participants perform a different search task, whereas completely irrelevant categories are no longer decodable.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion from the decoding results during Search 1 in Experiment 2.

claims.claim: Strong below-chance decoding was observed during Search 1 for the Current-Prospective cross-relevance classification in Experiment 2.
claims.source: Replicating Experiment 1, we observed strong below-chance decoding during Search 1 for the Current-Prospective cross-relevance classification (t(1, 24)=−5.92, p < 0.001, d = −1.18), while the Current-Irrelevant (t (1, 24)= −1.89, p = 0.071, d = −0.37) and the Prospective-Irrelevant (t(1,24) = 1.99, p = 0.058, d = 0.39) cross-decoding schemes did not significantly differ from chance.
claims.evidence: This is an fMRI decoding result from Experiment 2 with statistical support.

claims.claim: Decoding accuracy for the Current-Prospective scheme was significantly lower than for the Current-Irrelevant scheme during Search 1 in Experiment 2.
claims.source: Most importantly, decoding accuracy for the Current-Prospective scheme was significantly lower than for the Current-Irrelevant scheme (t(1,24) = −2.95, p = 0.007, d = −0.59), indicating that the Prospective condition involved a stronger representational transformation than the Irrelevant condition.
claims.evidence: This is an fMRI decoding result from Experiment 2 with statistical support.

claims.claim: The transformation of prospective representations is driven by the future relevance of the prospective template rather than by some passive, automatic mechanism.
claims.source: Since the prospective and irrelevant trials contained exactly the same visual input (see Methods), this result suggests that this transformation is driven by the future relevance of the prospective template rather than by some passive, automatic mechanism that would be the same for prospective and irrelevant representations (such as BOLD undershoot, see Discussion).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the differential decoding results between prospective and irrelevant conditions in Experiment 2.

claims.claim: Strong decoding of the category of the prospectively relevant target was observed during Search 2 when it had become task-relevant in Experiment 2.
claims.source: In line with Experiment 1, the pattern reversed for Search 2 (see Figure 4). In the within-relevance decoding scheme, we observed strong decoding of the category of the prospectively relevant target, which by now had become task-relevant (t(1,24) = 12.54, p < 0.001, d = 2.50), and decoding of the Prospective – now relevant - category was stronger than for the previously current – now no longer relevant – search target (t(1,23) = −8.84, p < 0.001, d = −1.76).
claims.evidence: This is an fMRI decoding result from Experiment 2 with statistical support and reference to Figure 4.

claims.claim: The current condition was at chance during Search 2 in Experiment 2.
claims.source: In contrast to Experiment 1, where we unexpectedly observed above-chance decoding for this no longer relevant target during Search 2, here the current condition was at chance (t(1,24) = 1.14, p = 0.265, d = 0.22).
claims.evidence: This is an fMRI decoding result from Experiment 2 with statistical support.

claims.claim: Below-chance decoding was found during Search 2 for the Current-Prospective cross-relevance decoding scheme in Experiment 2.
claims.source: However, similar to Experiment 1, we found below-chance decoding in the same time range for the Current-Prospective cross-relevance decoding scheme (vs. 33.3%: t(1,24) = −6.57 p < 0.001, d = −1.31), indicating that there was information present on the previously relevant target.
claims.evidence: This is an fMRI decoding result from Experiment 2 with statistical support.

claims.claim: In the Delay period, the neural representations of current and prospective targets of the same category were more similar than the representations of targets from different categories in Experiment 2.
claims.source: First, as can be seen in Figure 5A, B and C, we replicated the results from Experiment 1. In the Delay period, the neural representations of current and prospective targets of the same category were more similar (i.e., less dissimilarity) than the representations of targets from different categories (t(1,24) = −9.14, p < 0.001, d = −1.82, Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the representational dissimilarity analysis in Experiment 2 with reference to Figure 5.

claims.claim: During Search 1 and Search 2, currently and prospectively relevant objects from the same category were more dissimilar in Experiment 2.
claims.source: In contrast, during Search 1 and Search 2, currently and prospectively relevant objects from the same category were more dissimilar: As in Experiment 1, prospective targets differed most from current targets when they belonged to the same category than when they belonged to different categories (Search 1: t(1,24) = 5.20, p < 0.001, d = 1.04 and Search 2: t(1,24) = 6.45, p < 0.001, d = 1.29).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the representational dissimilarity analysis in Experiment 2 with statistical support.

claims.claim: Throughout the course of the trial, the neural representations of the target objects moved from predominantly category space in the Delay period prior to search to predominantly relevance space during the two searches in Experiment 2.
claims.source: Again, throughout the course of the trial, the neural representations of the target objects moved from predominantly category space in the Delay period prior to search to predominantly relevance space during the two searches, where current and prospective objects were represented in opposite corners of the representational space.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion from the representational dissimilarity analysis in Experiment 2.

claims.claim: For Irrelevant items, there was no evidence that the representations were warped in opposite corners of the multivariate space during Search 1 in Experiment 2.
claims.source: Importantly however, and in contrast to Prospective items, for Irrelevant items we did not find evidence that the representations were warped in opposite corners of the multivariate space during Search 1, as the (dis)similarity between targets belonging to the same or to different categories was equal for the Current-Irrelevant (t(1,24) = 0.94, p = 0.354, d = 0.89) and Prospective-Irrelevant (t(1,24) = −1.36, p = 0.184, d = −0.27) comparisons.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the representational dissimilarity analysis in Experiment 2 with statistical support.

claims.claim: Same category representations were relatively more dissimilar for Current-Prospective comparisons than for Current-Irrelevant and Prospective-Irrelevant comparisons in Experiment 2.
claims.source: This showed that same category representations were indeed relatively more dissimilar for Current-Prospective comparisons than for Current-Irrelevant (t(1,24) = 2.88, p = 0.008, d = 0.57) and Prospective-Irrelevant (t(1,24) = 4.69, p < 0.001, d = 0.93) comparisons.
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from the representational dissimilarity analysis in Experiment 2.

claims.claim: It is not the temporary irrelevance, but the prospective relevance that causes the representational transformation.
claims.source: Experiment 2 furthermore shows that it is not the temporary irrelevance, but the prospective relevance that causes this transformation, because little to no anti-correlation was found for items that were irrelevant altogether.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing prospective and irrelevant conditions in Experiment 2.

claims.claim: The transformation of prospective representations cannot be the result of basic stimulus-induced neural adaptation or BOLD response properties.
claims.source: Since prospective and irrelevant trials contained exactly the same visual input (up to Search 1 inclusive), the transformation of prospective representations cannot be the result of basic stimulus-induced neural adaptation or BOLD response properties.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental design of Experiment 2.

claims.claim: The content of working memory can be decoded from multivariate patterns of voxel activity when observers are remembering an item for a single task.
claims.source: It has been shown that the content of working memory can be decoded from multivariate patterns of voxel activity when observers are remembering an item for a single task (Albers et al., 2013; Harrison and Tong, 2009; Lewis-Peacock and Postle, 2012; Serences et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claims.claim: Working memory representations adapt to the specific task goal, as the representation of the same object changes depending on the nature of the upcoming test.
claims.source: Furthermore, working memory representations have been shown to adapt to the specific task goal, as the representation of the same object changes depending on the nature of the upcoming test (Lee et al., 2013; Myers et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claims.claim: Objects required for an upcoming search task are represented more strongly than when the same objects are only used prospectively or when they are completely irrelevant.
claims.source: In line with earlier work in different task and stimulus domains (LaRocque et al., 2013; LaRocque et al., 2017; Lewis-Peacock and Postle, 2012; Wolff et al., 2017), we observed that objects required for an upcoming search task are represented more strongly than when the same objects are only used prospectively (Experiment 1) or when they are completely irrelevant (Experiment 2), as was indicated by stronger classification performance in object-selective cortex prior to the first search.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of findings from both experiments with citations to related work.

claims.claim: The prospectively relevant memory could be reconstructed during task-irrelevant stimulation.
claims.source: Furthermore, corroborating findings by Rose et al. (2016), we observed that the prospectively relevant memory could be reconstructed during task-irrelevant stimulation, here during the first search for an unrelated stimulus.
claims.evidence: This finding corroborates prior work by Rose et al. (2016).

claims.claim: The results are the first to reveal a direct relationship between currently relevant object representations and prospective representations.
claims.source: Our results are the first to reveal a direct relationship between currently relevant object representations on the one hand, and prospective representations on the other.
claims.evidence: This claims novelty for the current findings.

claims.claim: Prior to the first search, current, prospective and irrelevant representations were very similar.
claims.source: Prior to the first search current, prospective and irrelevant representations were very similar, as cross-relevance decoding (training on one status while testing on the other) showed above-chance performance for all classification schemes and there were no differences across conditions.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of findings from the cross-relevance decoding analysis.

claims.claim: While the representation for prospective objects clearly reversed during search, such a reversal was weak to absent for irrelevant objects.
claims.source: However, while the representation for prospective objects clearly reversed during search, such a reversal was weak to absent for irrelevant objects.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of findings comparing prospective and irrelevant conditions.

claims.claim: During search, the reconstructed prospective memory representations of objects proved dissimilar from their current counterparts.
claims.source: We observed that during search, the reconstructed prospective memory representations of objects proved dissimilar from their current counterparts.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the main finding.

claims.claim: Prospective representations were even more dissimilar from current representations of the same object category than representations of a different object category.
claims.source: Importantly, they differed in a systematic manner, to the extent that prospective representations were even more dissimilar from current representations of the same object category than representations of a different object category, and were characterized by an inverse correlation with current representations.
claims.evidence: This is a key finding about the nature of the dissimilarity.

claims.claim: While irrelevant targets simply appeared to decay from memory, prospective target memories were transformed.
claims.source: Thus, while irrelevant targets simply appeared to decay from memory, prospective target memories were transformed.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion comparing the fate of irrelevant versus prospective representations.

claims.claim: Similar findings have been reported by Yu and Postle (2018) for a different stimulus class and a different brain area.
claims.source: We point out that similar (as yet unpublished) findings have recently been reported by Yu and Postle (2018), for a different stimulus class and a different brain area.
claims.evidence: This references convergent findings from another study.

claims.claim: Prospective targets may be dissociated from current targets in that current representations are activity-based, whereas prospective representations are responsivity-based.
claims.source: Together with our findings, these results indicate that prospective targets may be dissociated from current targets in two ways. First, they appear distinct in that current representations are activity-based, whereas prospective representations are responsivity-based.
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation of the findings.

claims.claim: Prospective targets are represented through a responsivity pattern different to that of current target activity, where the most active part becomes the relatively least responsive and vice versa.
claims.source: Second, prospective targets are represented through a responsivity pattern different to that of current target activity, where the most active part becomes the relatively least responsive and vice versa.

results.result: Two experiments were conducted with appropriate sample sizes (N=24 and N=25) using a dual visual search task where participants remembered object categories (cow, dresser, skate) as targets for consecutive searches.
results.evaluation: The experimental design is clearly described with adequate sample sizes for fMRI studies. The task structure is well-defined and appropriate for testing the research question about current versus prospective memory representations.

results.result: During the delay period prior to search, object category representations were decodable for current, prospective, and irrelevant items, with similar representational patterns across relevance conditions but stronger decoding for currently relevant items.
results.evaluation: Multiple statistical tests with appropriate corrections support above-chance decoding for all conditions during the delay. Cross-relevance decoding confirms representational similarity. The pattern is consistent across both experiments, though Experiment 2 showed no significant difference between current and prospective conditions.

results.result: During the first search, prospective category representations could be decoded above chance while participants searched for a different current target, whereas irrelevant representations remained at chance.
results.evaluation: Statistical tests demonstrate above-chance decoding of prospective representations during Search 1 in both experiments (C40: t(1,23)=1.90, p=0.035; C65: t(1,24)=3.35, p=0.003). Critically, Experiment 2 shows irrelevant items remain at chance (C66), confirming specificity to prospective relevance.

results.result: Current and prospective representations of the same object category showed anti-correlated (below-chance) cross-relevance decoding during search, indicating opposite multivariate patterns that are driven by future relevance rather than passive mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Below-chance cross-relevance decoding is statistically robust in both experiments (C42, C68). Critically, C69 shows Current-Prospective decoding was significantly lower than Current-Irrelevant, and C70 correctly notes identical visual input rules out passive mechanisms. This is the key novel finding.

results.result: Representational dissimilarity analysis in Experiment 1 revealed that neural representations transitioned from category-based organization during delay to relevance-based organization during search, with same-category current and prospective items becoming maximally dissimilar.
results.evaluation: Multiple statistical tests support the transition from category to relevance space (C53, C54, C55 all p<0.005). MDS plots (Figure 3) visually confirm opposite corners for same-category different-relevance items. The pattern is internally consistent and well-documented.

results.result: Experiment 2 replicated the representational transformation for prospective items but showed no such transformation for irrelevant items, demonstrating that prospective relevance specifically drives the anti-correlation pattern.
results.evaluation: Statistical tests confirm replication of Experiment 1 patterns for current-prospective comparisons (C74, C75) but crucially show no transformation for irrelevant items (C77, C78). Since visual input was identical for prospective and irrelevant conditions, this rules out sensory explanations (C80).

results.result: During the second search, the now-relevant prospective target showed strong decoding, while evidence for the no-longer-relevant first target showed below-chance cross-relevance decoding, suggesting a shared mechanism for preventing interference from both past and future targets.
results.evaluation: Statistical support is provided for both the reactivation of prospective targets (C46, C71) and the anti-correlation of no-longer-relevant targets (C48, C73). The pattern suggests bidirectional interference prevention (C102), though the unexpected above-chance decoding in Experiment 1 (C47) requires further investigation.

results.result: Behavioral results from Experiment 2 showed equal accuracy but slower reaction times for prospective versus current template searches, suggesting intact memory quality but additional reactivation time.
results.evaluation: The behavioral pattern is clearly described and the interpretation (C58, C59) is reasonable given the data. However, the claims are somewhat inferential - equal accuracy doesn't definitively prove no decay, and slower RT could have alternative explanations beyond reactivation time.

results.result: The brain separates current from prospective memories within the same neuronal ensembles through opposite representational patterns, where prospective representations are activity-silent and responsivity-based with inverted patterns relative to current active representations.
results.evaluation: This is the main theoretical conclusion synthesizing the empirical findings. The data strongly support opposite patterns within the same brain regions (C107-C108). The activity-silent interpretation (C92, C93, C112-C113) is well-reasoned given the need for external stimulation to reveal prospective representations, though the exact mechanism remains speculative.

results.result: The representational transformation cannot be explained by passive mechanisms like neural adaptation or BOLD undershoot, nor by simple reduced activity accounts, as evidenced by goal-state-dependent differences and anti-correlation patterns.
results.evaluation: The experimental design of Experiment 2 with identical visual input for prospective and irrelevant conditions (C105) provides strong evidence against passive sensory mechanisms (C104, C106). The anti-correlation pattern (C111, C114) argues against simple reduced activity (C110) and challenges synaptic potentiation models (C115).

results.result: The exact mechanism behind the transformation remains unknown, though active cognitive control from frontal areas is proposed as one possibility.
results.evaluation: The authors appropriately acknowledge this limitation (C96). The proposed mechanism (C97, C98) is speculative and not directly tested. The difference between experiments in delay period decoding (C95) suggests task-specific factors but the explanation is post-hoc.

results.result: The findings replicate and extend prior work showing stronger representations for current versus prospective items, reconstruction of prospective memories during task-irrelevant stimulation, and initial similarity followed by transformation of prospective representations.
results.evaluation: The claims appropriately cite relevant prior work (C83, C84) and the current findings are consistent with and extend this literature. The characterization of the temporal dynamics (C86, C87, C109) accurately summarizes the cross-relevance decoding results.
